items.title: COP17: Key outcomes agreed at the UN biodiversity conference in Yerevan
items.author: Carbon Brief Staff
items.summary: Nations at the COP17 biodiversity conference in Yerevan completed a global review warning that nature loss targets for 2030 are currently off track. brief.what: Delegates at COP17 completed a global review confirming that 2030 nature loss targets will not be met without accelerated action. The conference reached a compromise on resource mobilization, establishing a process for countries to voluntarily signal interest in contributing to biodiversity finance before COP18.
brief.who: The JUSCANZ bloc of developed countries led the push to broaden the contributor base, while emerging economies like China, Saudi Arabia, and India resisted mandatory reclassification.
brief.context: The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, established in 2022, aims to reverse nature loss by 2030. Finance has been a point of contention, as developed nations failed to meet previous funding commitments of at least $20bn annually.
brief.why: The deadlock occurred because developed countries sought to expand the list of nations responsible for providing finance, while developing nations argued that historical responsibilities and sovereign debt burdens should be prioritized over income-based status.
brief.next: Countries will hold bilateral, confidential consultations regarding donor status before COP18, which is scheduled to take place in Quito, Ecuador, in 2028.

items.summary: Two employees at the Armagh Observatory and Planetarium have had asteroids officially named after them in recognition of their contributions to space science and meteorology. The naming process is overseen by the International Astronomical Union, which allows discoverers to name asteroids once their orbits are confirmed.

brief.what: Dr. Rok Nežič and Shane Kelly have had asteroids named in their honor, specifically (20560) Nežič and (7050) Shanekelly. The Armagh Observatory and Planetarium plans to install a new LED dome to display these asteroids and their respective orbits.
brief.who: Dr. Rok Nežič, a tours and outreach officer, and Shane Kelly, the principal meteorological observer at Armagh Observatory and Planetarium, are the two individuals honored.
brief.context: The International Astronomical Union governs the naming of small solar system bodies. Asteroids are typically named by their discoverers once their orbital paths are sufficiently mapped.
brief.why: The honors recognize the individuals' contributions to the institution, with Nežič noted for his space and climate physics research and Kelly for his extensive meteorological data collection spanning 27 years.
brief.next: The institution plans to feature the asteroids in a new LED dome display.

items.summary: United MileagePlus uses dynamic pricing for business class awards, meaning there is no fixed mileage cost for a Polaris seat. Cardholders and Premier members can access exclusive inventory and receive percentage-based discounts, though availability remains capacity-controlled.

brief.what: United Airlines utilizes dynamic pricing for its MileagePlus program, resulting in variable costs for Polaris business class seats rather than a fixed award chart. While baseline Saver Award seats start at 80,000 miles, costs fluctuate based on demand and inventory. Cardholders and Premier members gain access to exclusive Saver inventory and receive discounts of 10% to 15% on eligible flights.

brief.context: United's loyalty program shifted toward dynamic pricing, where award costs are determined by market factors rather than static tables. The airline recently expanded access to previously restricted Polaris Saver inventory to include all credit and debit cardholders.
brief.why: United implemented these changes to provide tiered benefits to cardholders and frequent flyers, though the airline emphasizes that these figures are illustrative examples rather than guaranteed rates.

items.summary: Authorities have concluded there was no foul play in the death of a 32-year-old Nvidia AI prodigy. Despite this, supporters in Silicon Valley and Bangladesh continue to question the circumstances surrounding the case.

brief.what: Authorities have officially found no evidence of foul play regarding the death of a 32-year-old Nvidia AI prodigy. The investigation into the individual's passing has reached this conclusion, though the case remains a subject of intense scrutiny.
brief.who: The deceased individual was a 32-year-old AI prodigy formerly associated with Nvidia, while authorities are the entities responsible for the investigation.

items.title: How one family gave a critical boost to gene therapy research
items.author: Sydney Lupkin
items.summary: The FDA has approved a gene therapy for Sanfilippo syndrome, a rare inherited disease, following years of research funded by patient families and foundations. The treatment, known as Fayuvi, is priced at nearly $4 million.

brief.what: The FDA approved Fayuvi, a gene therapy for Sanfilippo syndrome, a rare metabolic disorder. The treatment, which costs nearly $4 million, was developed after years of research supported by patient families and foundations.
brief.who: The O'Neill family, researcher Haiyan Fu, and the biotech company Ultragenyx are the primary actors who advanced the therapy from early research to commercial approval.
brief.context: Sanfilippo syndrome is a rare inherited disease where a faulty gene prevents the breakdown of heparin sulfate, leading to severe neurological degeneration. Patients typically do not survive past their teens.
brief.why: The research was sustained by patient foundations when funding was scarce, and the O'Neill family raised significant capital through viral crowdfunding. Ultragenyx later acquired the rights and submitted data to the FDA.
brief.next: Ultragenyx states it is committed to ensuring patients receive the treatment regardless of logistical or location-based barriers.
